t-moe.overview: **Mixture of Experts** is the idea that lets a model's knowledge capacity grow without its per-token cost growing with it. The [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) in each transformer layer is split into many parallel sub-networks, and a small [router](#c/router) sends each token to only a few of them, so a model like [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) holds 671B parameters but does arithmetic with about 37B per token. This topic traces the idea from the [1991 'Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts' paper](#c/moe-1991) through [sparse gating in 2017](#c/sparse-moe), [GShard](#c/gshard) and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch), to the balancing and granularity fixes ([auxiliary loss](#c/lb-loss), [loss-free bias balancing](#c/aux-free), [fine-grained plus shared experts](#c/fine-grained)) that made it the open-weight default by 2025. It also corrects two common misconceptions: that experts are topic specialists, and that MoE is a recent breakthrough rather than a decade of incremental engineering on a 1991 idea.

t-models.overview: This topic surveys what published models are actually made of, from the dense scaling era to the MoE-dominated open landscape of 2025–26. Parameter counts rose 1000× from [GPT-1](#c/gpt-1) (117M) to [GPT-3](#c/gpt-3) (175B) in two years, then about 10× more to an estimated ~1.8T for [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4). After that the trend [reversed](#c/r-smaller): frontier models got smaller, and [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) split *total* parameters (capacity) from *active* ones (cost). The open flagships, among them [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4), [Qwen3](#c/qwen3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-5](#c/glm-5), all use MoE, but they differ on expert granularity, whether to keep a shared expert, and attention type (GQA, MLA, sparse or linear). A recurring lesson is that [recent architecture changes mostly bought efficiency](#c/c-arch-efficiency), while the quality gains came from post-training. Newer releases (GLM-5.1, GLM-5.2) come with self-reported and sometimes contradictory benchmark claims.

moe.overview: **Mixture of Experts (MoE)** replaces a transformer layer's single [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) with many parallel FFN blocks, called "experts". A tiny learned [router](#c/router) scores every expert for each token, keeps the top-k, and sums their outputs weighted by those scores. Attention stays dense and shared. This decouples *total* parameters, which set knowledge capacity, from *active* parameters, which set compute per token: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) stores 671B but activates about 37B (8 of 256 routed experts plus 1 shared, in 58 of its 61 layers). Routing is re-decided for every token at every MoE layer, and experts learn low-level token patterns, [not human topics](#c/r-experts). The costs are memory, since every expert must sit in HBM, cross-GPU communication, and the need to keep load balanced. MoE dates to [1991](#c/moe-1991) and became the open-weight default in 2025.
moe.article:
**Mixture of Experts (MoE)** is a neural-network design in which only part of the model runs for any given input. In modern large language models, it means splitting each transformer layer's [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) into many smaller, parallel "experts" and letting a learned [router](#c/router) send each token to just a few of them. The result is a model with the *capacity* of its total parameter count and roughly the *running cost* of its much smaller active parameter count. By 2025 it had become the default architecture for large open-weight models, including [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Llama 4](#c/llama4), [Qwen3](#c/qwen3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-5](#c/glm-5).

## How it works

A transformer layer has two main parts: attention, where tokens look at one another, and a feed-forward network that processes each token on its own. MoE replaces **only the FFN**. Attention stays dense, and every token still uses all of it. So when a model is described as having "256 experts", that means its FFN block has been split into 256 parallel weight-blocks. It does not mean 256 small models.

In front of the experts sits the router, which is essentially a single learned linear layer. For each token's hidden vector it produces a score for every expert (a dot product with that expert's routing vector) and turns the scores into weights. The token is sent to the top-k experts, and their outputs are combined using those weights and added back into the [residual stream](#c/residual). Routing is decided **fresh for every token, independently, at every MoE layer**. DeepSeek-V3 has 58 MoE layers, so a single token passes through 58 separate routing decisions, and the next token gets its own 58.

## Total vs. active parameters

In a dense model every parameter fires on every token, so compute scales with size. MoE breaks that link:

| Model | Total | Active per token | Routed experts |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V3 | 671B | ~37B | 256 (8 + 1 shared active) |
| Llama 4 Maverick | 400B | 17B | 128 |
| Kimi K2 | ~1T | 32B | 384 |
| GLM-5 | 744B | ~40B | 256 (8 active) |

This is why the phrase "parameter count" became ambiguous after 2023 and why [frontier models could shrink in active size](#c/r-smaller) even as totals climbed. Because active parameters set the arithmetic per token, MoE directly lowers [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) at a given capability.

## What experts specialize in

Inspections of trained routers usually find that experts specialise in **low-level patterns**: token types, punctuation, number-like tokens and structural roles. They rarely specialise in human topics like "chemistry" or "law". The popular picture of a question activating "the chemistry expert" is [appealing but mostly false](#c/m-experts). Routing distributes computational sub-patterns rather than dispatching to topic specialists.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Load balancing.** Left alone, routing collapses. Experts picked slightly more often early in training get better and are then picked even more, which leaves a few overworked experts and many dead ones. The classic fix is an [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), often combined with an expert-capacity cap that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. DeepSeek later introduced [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) using per-expert bias terms.
- **Memory.** Every expert must be stored. All 671B of DeepSeek-V3's parameters sit in expensive HBM even though most are idle for any given token, which ties MoE to the [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound) nature of inference.
- **Communication.** When experts are spread across GPUs, tokens have to be shipped to wherever their chosen experts live. GLM-5 cut its depth to 80 layers partly to reduce this expert-parallel traffic.
- **Design questions that are still open.** Labs disagree on granularity (many small experts, as in DeepSeek's [fine-grained design](#c/fine-grained), or a few large ones, as in Llama 4) and on whether to keep an always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). [Qwen3 dropped it](#c/no-shared).

## History

The idea is old. It dates to [Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton in 1991](#c/moe-1991). [Sparse gating in deep networks](#c/sparse-moe) arrived in 2017 (Shazeer et al., up to 137B parameters), the same year as the Transformer. [GShard](#c/gshard) brought it into the Transformer in 2020 at more than 600B parameters, and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) simplified routing to a single expert per token in 2021. What turned the idea into the thing running most open flagships was a decade of [incremental fixes](#c/c-incremental): balancing losses, capacity limits, routing-stability work, shared experts and expert-sharding systems.

## From the chat

- MoE "flips on every single token, and that's not a quirk, it's the whole design". Routing is re-decided per token and per layer.
- The chat corrected the "topic expert" intuition: an expert is just one of N parallel FFN weight-blocks, and specialisation is low-level and "alien to how a human would carve up knowledge".
- MoE is [not a recent breakthrough](#c/r-moe-old). The idea is from 1991 and sparse gating from 2017. Its value came from years of incremental engineering, which is why the chat treated it as evidence that cost declines come mostly from accumulated tweaks.
- The chat declined to attribute Epoch's measured cost drop to MoE alone. MoE is one ingredient in a ~3×/year algorithmic-efficiency slice.
- The routing schemes inside closed models such as Claude and GPT are not disclosed. They are broadly understood to be MoE, but the exact variant isn't known.

moe-1991.overview: **"Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts"** (Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton, *Neural Computation*, 1991) is where the Mixture of Experts idea begins. It proposed training several separate networks (the experts) alongside a gating network that learns, for each input, how much to trust each expert. The experts compete to handle each case, which pushes them to divide the input space among themselves instead of all learning the same thing. In this original form every expert still computed on every input and the gate only reweighted their outputs, so it saved no compute. The step that makes modern [MoE](#c/moe) cheap is sparse top-k gating, which came from [Shazeer et al. in 2017](#c/sparse-moe). The chat used this date to [correct the belief](#c/r-moe-old) that MoE is a recent breakthrough: the core idea is more than three decades old.

sparse-moe.overview: The **Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer**, from Shazeer and colleagues at Google in the January 2017 paper "Outrageously Large Neural Networks", is the version of MoE that matters for modern LLMs. A trainable gate picks only the top few of many experts for each input, so compute per example stays roughly fixed while parameter count grows. That enabled models of up to **137 billion parameters** when that was enormous. The layers sat between recurrent (LSTM) layers and were tested on language modelling and machine translation. The paper also ran into the central problem of sparse routing, expert collapse, and added balancing penalties to fight it, the ancestor of the [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss). It appeared the same year as the Transformer. [GShard](#c/gshard) carried the idea into Transformers in 2020, and modern [MoE](#c/moe) descends from it.
sparse-moe.article:
The **Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer** was introduced by Noam Shazeer and colleagues at Google in the January 2017 paper *"Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer."* It took the [1991 mixture-of-experts idea](#c/moe-1991), made the gating **sparse** so that only a few experts run for each input, and put it inside a deep network. That broke the rule that more parameters means proportionally more compute, and it let the authors train models of up to **137 billion parameters**. Nearly every modern [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) LLM descends from this layer.

## How it works

The layer holds a large pool of expert networks, each a simple feed-forward block, and a gating network. For each input the gate computes a score per expert and keeps only the top-k, setting the rest to zero. Only the selected experts run, and their outputs are combined using the gate's weights. The paper added tunable noise to the gate scores before the top-k selection. The noise encourages exploration and helps spread load.

Since most experts are skipped for any given input, total parameters can grow by orders of magnitude while computation per example grows only a little. The paper called this "conditional computation" and presented it as the way past the compute limits of dense models.

## Architecture

The experiments predate the Transformer's dominance. The MoE layers were placed between stacked LSTM layers and applied to language modelling and machine translation. The design pattern is still the same one used today: a learned [router](#c/router) in front of a pool of [feed-forward](#c/ffn) experts.

## The balancing problem

The paper identified the failure mode that still shapes MoE design. Left to itself, the gate tends to converge on a few favourite experts. They get more training, so they improve, so they get picked more, and the rest of the pool is wasted. The authors added extra loss terms that penalise uneven expert usage. This is the ancestor of the [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), which was later refined and eventually replaced in DeepSeek's case by [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free).

## Why it matters

The 2017 paper came out the same year as the Transformer. From there the path runs through [GShard](#c/gshard) (2020), which put sparse MoE into the Transformer at more than 600B parameters, and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) (2021), which simplified routing to one expert per token. It then leads to the fine-grained, shared-expert designs of [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) and its peers. The key idea, that capacity can grow faster than cost, is the reason the total-versus-active split exists at all.

## Trade-offs and limits

Sparse gating makes computation cheap, but not memory or communication. Every expert still has to be stored, and on multi-device hardware tokens must be sent to wherever their chosen experts live. Training stability and load balance also needed years of further work. The chat's point was that the breakthrough came in 2017 but most of the value arrived later, through a long tail of [incremental engineering](#c/c-incremental).

## From the chat

- The chat dated "the version that matters for modern LLMs—sparse, gated, dropped into deep nets" to 2017, with the Shazeer et al. paper enabling models of up to 137B parameters.
- It noted that the paper is the same age as the Transformer, which means MoE's key innovations came well before the inference-price data window that Epoch measures (roughly April 2024 onward).
- It used the paper as the main example that "breakthrough vs. tweak" is a false binary. The idea came in 1991 and 2017, but almost none of the value was realised until later fixes made it trainable and servable.

gshard.overview: **GShard** (Lepikhin et al., Google, 2020) brought sparse [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) into the Transformer and scaled it past **600 billion parameters**, using multilingual machine translation as the test bed. It replaced the feed-forward block in every other Transformer layer with an MoE layer, routed each token to its top two experts, and put a cap on how many tokens each expert could take per batch, sending overflow onward without expert processing. Just as important was the systems side: GShard was an automatic sharding approach that spread experts across many accelerators, the start of the expert-parallel training that every large MoE now depends on. It sits between the [2017 sparsely-gated layer](#c/sparse-moe) and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch), which cut routing to a single expert per token in 2021.

switch.overview: The **Switch Transformer** (Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer, Google, 2021) simplified [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) routing to its limit: each token goes to **exactly one** expert (top-1) rather than two or more. That roughly halves routing computation and communication and makes each expert's batch smaller and more predictable. The authors paired it with an expert *capacity factor* (a buffer on how many tokens each expert accepts, with overflow passed through untouched), a simplified [load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), and stability tricks such as computing the router in higher precision. It pushed sparse models toward a trillion parameters, with a 1.6T-parameter model, and reported large pre-training speedups over dense T5 baselines at equal compute. Later designs went the other way on granularity: DeepSeek's [fine-grained experts](#c/fine-grained) route each token to many small experts instead of one large one.
switch.article:
The **Switch Transformer**, published by William Fedus, Barret Zoph and Noam Shazeer at Google in 2021, showed that sparse [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) routing could be made radically simpler. Where earlier designs sent each token to its top two or more experts, Switch sends each token to **exactly one**. The paper argued that this top-1 "switch" routing keeps model quality while cutting routing cost, communication and implementation complexity, and it used the approach to push sparse Transformers toward trillion-parameter scale.

## How it works

Switch follows the standard MoE pattern: the [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) in a Transformer layer is replaced by a pool of experts, and a learned [router](#c/router) scores each expert for each token. Switch keeps only the single highest-scoring expert and scales its output by the router's probability, so the router still gets a gradient.

Top-1 routing has several practical benefits:

- **Less computation in the router** and fewer expert calls per token.
- **Smaller expert batches**, because each token occupies one slot and not two.
- **Simpler communication** when experts are spread across devices.

## Capacity and balancing

Hardware needs fixed tensor shapes, so each expert gets a fixed *capacity*: the number of tokens it can accept per batch, set by a **capacity factor** multiplied by an even share of the batch. Tokens routed to an expert that is already full overflow and pass through the layer unprocessed via the residual connection. A capacity factor above 1 gives some slack at the cost of wasted compute.

To keep routing balanced, Switch uses a simplified [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss). It penalises the product of the fraction of tokens each expert receives and the router probability assigned to it, pushing both toward uniform. The paper also addressed training instability with selective precision: the router runs in float32 while the rest of the model uses bfloat16. It also used smaller initialisation and more dropout inside experts during fine-tuning.

## Scale and results

The paper scaled to a **1.6-trillion-parameter** model and reported substantial pre-training speedups over dense T5 baselines trained with the same compute per token. Those results cemented the point that sparse models could turn extra parameters into quality without extra per-token arithmetic.

## Why it matters

Switch is the step between [GShard](#c/gshard) (2020, top-2 routing past 600B parameters) and the modern open-weight MoE era. It established the vocabulary later work took for granted: capacity factors, token dropping, router precision and a simple balancing loss.

## Trade-offs and limits

Top-1 routing gives each token only one expert's view per layer, and dropped tokens mean some computation is skipped. Later designs moved the other way on granularity. DeepSeek's [fine-grained experts](#c/fine-grained) split capacity into many small experts and route each token to several (8 of 256 in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3)), plus an always-on shared expert. That arrangement gives the router finer-grained combinations to choose from. [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) sits nearer the Switch end, with few large experts active per token. The capacity and dropping machinery was also partly superseded: DeepSeek-V3 reports dropping no tokens, relying on [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) instead.

## From the chat

- The chat described Switch as the 2021 step that "simplified routing to a single expert per token and pushed toward trillion-parameter models".
- It listed "the top-1 simplification" among the incremental fixes that together turned MoE from a clever idea into the architecture behind most frontier models.
- The chat noted that router top-k is "usually 1 or 2" in the classic picture. Modern fine-grained designs like DeepSeek-V3 use 8 routed experts, and the gap shows how far the field moved after Switch.

lb-loss.overview: The **auxiliary load-balancing loss** is an extra training penalty that stops a [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) [router](#c/router) from collapsing onto a few favourite experts. Without it, training falls into a feedback loop: experts picked slightly more often early on get more gradient updates, improve, get picked even more, and leave the rest of the pool dead, wasting most of the model's capacity. The loss grows when routing is lopsided. In the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) form it multiplies each expert's share of tokens by its average router probability, pushing both toward uniform. It usually comes with an expert-capacity cap that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. The tension is that pushing too hard for balance can erase useful specialisation and hurt quality. That penalty is what DeepSeek's [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) was designed to avoid. The idea traces back to the [2017 sparsely-gated MoE paper](#c/sparse-moe).

aux-free.overview: **Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** is DeepSeek's alternative to the [auxiliary balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), and it shipped in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) (December 2024). Each expert gets a bias term that is added to its router score *only when choosing the top-k experts*. After each training step the bias goes down for overloaded experts and up for underused ones, so traffic evens out. The gating weights that combine expert outputs still come from the unbiased token-expert affinity. Balancing is therefore done by a simple controller, without a gradient-carrying loss that fights the language-modelling objective, and DeepSeek reports it avoids the quality penalty such losses impose. In the public V3 config it shows up as `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` ("no aux" meaning no auxiliary loss) with `scoring_func: "sigmoid"`.
aux-free.article:
**Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** is a technique for keeping [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) routing balanced without adding a penalty term to the training loss. DeepSeek researchers introduced it in 2024 and used it at scale in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) (December 2024). It replaces the conventional [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss) with per-expert bias terms that steer which experts get chosen. The aim is to keep all experts in use without the quality loss an auxiliary loss can cause.

## The problem it solves

An MoE [router](#c/router) left alone tends to collapse. A few experts win early, get more training, and end up handling most tokens while the rest sit idle. The standard remedy is an auxiliary loss that penalises uneven routing. That loss sends its own gradients into the router and the model, and those gradients pull against the actual language-modelling objective. Set the penalty weight too low and the load stays unbalanced. Set it too high and quality suffers, because the router is pushed away from the experts that suit each token best.

## How it works

The method separates *which experts are selected* from *how their outputs are weighted*:

1. The router computes an affinity score between the token and each expert. In DeepSeek-V3 this uses a sigmoid rather than a softmax.
2. A per-expert **bias** is added to these scores, but **only for top-k selection**. The token goes to the 8 experts with the highest biased scores.
3. The **gating weights** used to combine the selected experts' outputs come from the original, unbiased affinities.
4. After each training step, each expert's bias is nudged by a fixed small amount: down if the expert was overloaded, up if it was underloaded.

This amounts to a feedback controller placed next to the model, not a term inside the loss. No balancing gradient flows through the network, so the model's parameters are shaped only by the real training objective, while the biases quietly move traffic around.

DeepSeek-V3's technical report says it also kept a very small sequence-level balance loss as a backstop against extreme imbalance within a single sequence. The main mechanism is still the bias. The report also describes routing with no token dropping during training or inference, which older capacity-capped designs like the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) relied on.

## In the config

The public DeepSeek-V3 `config.json` exposes the technique directly: `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` ("noaux" meaning no auxiliary loss) and `scoring_func: "sigmoid"`. DeepSeek-V3 combines it with [fine-grained and shared experts](#c/fine-grained): 256 routed experts, 8 active per token, plus 1 shared expert.

## Why it matters

Load balancing is one of the long-running engineering problems that decided whether MoE was practical. Auxiliary-loss-free balancing is a good example of the [incremental fixes](#c/c-incremental) that unlocked MoE's value years after the idea itself. It adds nothing at inference, costs almost nothing in training, and removes a trade-off between hardware efficiency and model quality.

## Trade-offs and limits

The bias update is a hand-tuned controller with its own step-size hyperparameter. Because balance is enforced over batches, individual sequences can still be lopsided, which is why a small complementary loss was kept. The approach also assumes the router's affinity scores are worth protecting from interference, meaning some useful specialisation exists. That specialisation is [low-level rather than topical](#c/r-experts).

## From the chat

- The chat described it as DeepSeek's answer to the balancing problem: "adjusting per-expert bias terms to balance load without the performance penalty of an auxiliary loss, while keeping the actual gating based on pure token-expert affinity."
- When it walked through DeepSeek-V3's real `config.json`, it tied `scoring_func: "sigmoid"` and `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` to this technique, reading "noaux" as literally "no auxiliary loss".
- It placed the technique in the wider balancing tension: balance the load enough to use every parameter, but not so hard that you destroy the useful specialisation the router has learned.

fine-grained.overview: **Fine-grained plus shared experts** is DeepSeek's MoE layout, introduced in its DeepSeekMoE work in 2024 and used in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3). Instead of a few large experts, capacity is cut into **many small ones**. V3 has 256 routed experts, each with an intermediate width of only 2048, smaller than the 7168-wide hidden state, where a dense FFN would usually be several times wider. Each token activates 8 of them. With more, smaller experts to pick from, the router has far more possible combinations. On top of that sits one **[shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c)** that every token always uses. It captures common, general-purpose processing so the routed experts don't each have to relearn it. [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and GLM-4.5 kept this pattern. [Llama 4](#c/llama4) went the other way with few large experts, and [Qwen3 dropped the shared expert](#c/no-shared), so the question is still open.
fine-grained.article:
**Fine-grained plus shared experts** is a way of organising a [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) layer that DeepSeek popularised with its DeepSeekMoE work in 2024 and carried into [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) and [V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32). It makes two changes to the classic design. First, **fine-grained segmentation**: split the expert capacity into many small experts and activate several per token, not a few large ones. Second, **shared-expert isolation**: set aside one or more experts that every token always uses. The layout has spread widely. [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and GLM-4.5 both use it.

## How it works

In a classic MoE such as the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch), each expert is a full-size FFN and a token goes to one or two of them. Fine-grained MoE keeps the parameter budget but divides it into smaller pieces. Concretely, in DeepSeek-V3:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Hidden size (`hidden_size`) | 7168 |
| Dense FFN intermediate (first 3 layers) | 18432 |
| Expert intermediate (`moe_intermediate_size`) | 2048 |
| Routed experts | 256 |
| Routed experts per token | 8 |
| Shared experts | 1 |

A token entering an MoE layer is scored by the [router](#c/router). It goes to 8 of the [256 routed experts](#c/experts), and each of those computes 7168 → 2048 → 7168 with its own weights. Their outputs, plus the shared expert's, are summed back into the [residual stream](#c/residual). That is why "9 active experts" sometimes appears in write-ups: 8 routed plus 1 shared.

The notable detail is the width. In a dense transformer the FFN's middle layer is usually several times *wider* than the hidden size, as with V3's own dense layers at about 2.6×. The experts here are deliberately *narrower* than the hidden size, and that is the design choice.

## Why many small experts

Picking 8 of 256 gives vastly more possible expert combinations than picking 1 or 2 of 8 or 16. The router can put together a more specific mix for each token, and each expert can specialise more narrowly. The active compute is similar to a coarser design with the same active parameter count, but the model's knowledge is split into finer pieces.

## Why a shared expert

Some processing is needed by almost every token. Without a shared expert, many routed experts would each learn a redundant copy of these basics, which wastes capacity. An always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) handles the common part, so the routed experts can concentrate on what varies.

## Adoption and divergence

This is where open-model designs split in 2025:

- **Kept both ideas:** DeepSeek-V3/V3.2, Kimi K2 (384 routed experts, an even sparser configuration) and GLM-4.5.
- **Fewer, larger experts:** [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) uses 128 experts with 2 active per token at an 8192 width, and alternates MoE and dense layers.
- **Dropped the shared expert:** [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) removed it. The chat called this [one of the unsettled questions in MoE design](#c/no-shared).

## Trade-offs and limits

More, smaller experts mean more routing decisions, more small matrix multiplications that are harder to run efficiently, and heavier all-to-all communication when experts are spread across GPUs. GLM-5, which also uses 256 experts, reduced its layer count to 80 partly to limit expert-parallel traffic. The shared expert's value is also disputed: Qwen3's results suggest a strong model can do without it.

## From the chat

- The chat introduced shared experts as "a newer refinement... DeepSeek popularized": always-on experts that capture general processing, so routed experts don't "redundantly relearn the basics".
- It pointed out that DeepSeek's expert intermediate width (2048) is *smaller* than the hidden size (7168), "backwards from a normal FFN and... the whole point of fine-grained MoE."
- It framed the DeepSeek-versus-Llama 4 contrast as two MoE philosophies: many small experts against few large 8192-wide ones.
- It corrected a typo in the user's question: the hidden size is 7168, not 716.

no-shared.overview: **Dropping the shared expert** is the MoE design choice [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) made in April 2025. Its MoE layers have only routed experts, with no always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). DeepSeek's [fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained) layout had made a shared expert look standard: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45) all kept one, arguing that it absorbs common processing so routed experts don't each relearn the basics. Qwen3 removing it, while still ranking at the top of its size classes, suggests the shared expert may not be necessary, or that its benefit can be recovered through other choices such as expert count and training setup. The chat called this "one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design right now," and for now it stands as a live experiment, not a settled result.

gpt-1.overview: **GPT-1** (OpenAI, 2018) was a **117-million-parameter** decoder-only transformer, and it marks the start of the dense scaling era. It showed that generative pre-training on unlabelled text, followed by fine-tuning, transfers well to downstream language tasks, which is the recipe every later GPT followed. Like all models of its time it was dense: every parameter ran on every token, so size and per-token cost moved together. It is the baseline for one of the steepest scale-ups in computing. In two years parameters rose [1000× to GPT-3](#c/e-params-dense)'s 175B, and then roughly 10× more to [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4)'s estimated 1.8T, before the trend [reversed after 2023](#c/r-smaller) and [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) separated total parameters from active ones.

gpt-3.overview: **GPT-3** (OpenAI, 2020) was a dense **175-billion-parameter** transformer, about [1000× larger than GPT-1](#c/e-params-dense) only two years earlier. Its lasting result was few-shot, in-context learning: a model big enough could perform new tasks from a handful of examples in the prompt, without fine-tuning. It is the high point of the "bigger is better" era, when parameter count was the main lever on capability and every parameter fired on every token. Two developments broke that link soon afterward. [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla) (2022) showed models like GPT-3 were undertrained, at roughly 20 tokens per parameter as the compute-optimal target, and [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) decoupled capacity from per-token cost. GPT-3 to [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) was a further [~10× step](#c/e-params-gpt4) over about 2¾ years.

gpt-4.overview: **GPT-4** (OpenAI, March 2023) is the peak of the parameter-scaling era. OpenAI has never disclosed its size. The widely cited **~1.8 trillion** figure is an estimate built on leaks and analyst inference, as is the commonly reported claim that it is a Mixture of Experts, so treat both as unconfirmed. If the pre-2023 trend had continued, frontier models would be near 10T parameters by now. Instead, per Epoch's analysis, sizes [reversed](#c/r-smaller): GPT-4o is estimated at ~200B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet at ~400B, [about 10× smaller](#c/e-params-shrink), and neither lab has confirmed either figure. The chat attributes the reversal to [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla)-style data scaling and to [MoE](#c/moe) separating total from active parameters. This is why the idea that [frontier models keep getting bigger](#c/m-bigger) is a misconception.

deepseek-v3.overview: **DeepSeek-V3** (December 2024) is the most thoroughly documented open MoE flagship: **671B total, ~37B active** per token. Its public config gives 61 layers (3 dense, then 58 MoE), hidden size 7168, and [256 routed experts](#c/experts) of width 2048, with 8 routed plus 1 [shared expert](#c/fine-grained) active per token. It also has 128 attention heads, a 129,280-token vocabulary and 160K context via [YaRN](#c/yarn). It combines three distinctive techniques. [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla) caches a 512-dim latent instead of full K/V, about 32× smaller. [Auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) replaces the balancing loss with per-expert biases. [Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp) adds a causal extra-token training objective that can double as a speculative-decoding head. It was trained natively in FP8 and ships FP8 weights. The weights and inference code are open, but the training data and full orchestration are not.
deepseek-v3.article:
**DeepSeek-V3** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) language model released by the Chinese lab DeepSeek in December 2024. With **671 billion total parameters and about 37 billion active per token**, it became the reference example of an MoE model's "huge capacity, modest running cost" trade. It is also the best-documented open flagship: its technical report and public `config.json` specify the architecture exactly. The same backbone underlies the reasoning model [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1) and the later [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32).

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Total / active parameters | 671B / ~37B |
| Layers | 61 (first 3 dense, then 58 MoE) |
| Hidden size | 7168 |
| Dense FFN intermediate | 18432 |
| Routed experts | 256, intermediate width 2048 |
| Active experts per token | 8 routed + 1 shared |
| Attention | [MLA](#c/mla), 128 heads |
| KV latent (`kv_lora_rank`) | 512 |
| Query latent (`q_lora_rank`) | 1536 |
| Vocabulary | 129,280 |
| Context | 160K (163,840), via [YaRN](#c/yarn) from a 4,096 base |
| Precision | Native FP8 training and weights |

Each MoE layer sends every token to 8 of the [256 routed experts](#c/experts) and also to one always-on shared expert. That is the [fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained) layout. Each expert computes 7168 → 2048 → 7168, deliberately narrower than the hidden size.

## Distinctive techniques

**[Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)](#c/mla).** Instead of shrinking the number of key/value heads as [GQA](#c/gqa) does, MLA compresses keys and values into a shared low-rank latent and caches only that latent. The latent is 512-dimensional, against 128 heads × 128 = 16,384 for full K/V, about a 32× reduction in [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) size. The config lists 128 KV heads, which looks like full multi-head attention, because the compression is expressed elsewhere. [RoPE](#c/rope) doesn't survive the compression, so position is carried in a separate "decoupled" 64-dim slice alongside a 128-dim content part.

**[Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing](#c/aux-free).** Per-expert bias terms steer top-k selection toward underused experts, while the gating weights still come from the pure token-expert affinity. In the config: `scoring_func: "sigmoid"`, `topk_method: "noaux_tc"`.

**[Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)](#c/mtp).** During training the model also predicts further-ahead tokens, keeping a causal chain across prediction depths (`num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`). This gives a denser training signal, and the extra module can serve as a draft head for [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding).

**FP8.** DeepSeek trained natively in FP8 and publishes only FP8 weights (`quant_method: "fp8"`), with a script to convert to BF16. This ties it to wider work on [numeric precision](#c/weights-precision) and [quantization](#c/quantization).

## Openness

The weights are on Hugging Face and the inference code is open. DeepSeek also released parts of its training infrastructure, including DualPipe (a bidirectional pipeline-parallelism scheme that overlaps computation with communication) and an expert-parallel load balancer, and Hugging Face `transformers` has a native `deepseek_v3` implementation. What isn't released is the training data and the full pre-training orchestration, so reproducing it end to end from scratch isn't possible.

## Why it matters

V3 is the standard example of [total versus active parameters](#c/r-smaller). It has the knowledge capacity of 671B parameters and the per-token arithmetic of roughly 37B, which is why [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) could fall even as models' total sizes grew. Its techniques spread quickly: [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) borrowed MLA, and V3.2's sparse attention was taken up by [GLM-5](#c/glm-5).

## Trade-offs and limits

All 671B parameters must sit in accelerator memory even though most are idle on any given token, and routing tokens to experts on other GPUs adds communication overhead. MLA's cache savings come at the price of compression and decompression compute.

## From the chat

- The chat called V3 "the most thoroughly documented" open model and pulled the exact shape from the real `config.json` instead of relying on secondhand articles. That corrected earlier roundup figures: 61 layers, with the first 3 dense.
- It explained "9 active experts" as 8 routed plus 1 shared, and walked through why the 2048 expert width is smaller than the 7168 hidden size.
- It worked out MLA's memory saving from the config: a 512-dim cached latent against 16,384 for naive K/V, about 32× smaller.
- On openness: the architecture and inference are fully open, the training components partly so, and the data is not released. The chat said this is broadly the same for Llama 4, Qwen3 and Kimi K2.

deepseek-r1.overview: **DeepSeek-R1** (January 2025) is DeepSeek's reasoning model, built on the same **671B-total / 37B-active** MoE backbone as [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3): 61 layers, [MLA](#c/mla), 256 routed experts with 8 + 1 shared active. The architecture is unchanged. What's new is post-training. R1 showed that [RLVR](#c/rlvr), reinforcement learning against automatically checkable rewards for math and code, optimised with [GRPO](#c/grpo), can elicit long chain-of-thought reasoning, including a reported "aha moment" where the model spontaneously began to reflect on and revise its work. It reached this largely without distilling from a closed frontier model, which [cuts against the claim](#c/c-distill-open) that open reasoning gains mostly come from copying. DeepSeek then [distilled](#c/distillation) R1's reasoning into smaller open models. Whether RLVR creates [genuinely new ability](#c/c-rlvr-new) or sharpens latent ability is still debated.
deepseek-r1.article:
**DeepSeek-R1** is an open-weight reasoning model released by DeepSeek in January 2025. It became the landmark demonstration that **reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards** ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) can teach a large language model to reason step by step, producing long chains of thought and even spontaneous self-correction, without human-written reasoning traces for every step. Its architecture is the [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) backbone unchanged. Everything new about R1 is in [post-training](#c/post-training).

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Total / active parameters | 671B / ~37B |
| Layers | 61 |
| Experts | 256 routed, 8 + 1 shared active per token |
| Attention | [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla) |
| Base | DeepSeek-V3 |

Because the backbone is identical to V3, R1's jump in reasoning shows clearly that capability can come from training alone, with no architectural change.

## How it was trained

The central method is RLVR. Instead of rewarding the model with a learned reward model that stands in for human preferences, as in [RLHF](#c/rlhf), RLVR uses deterministic checks: does the math answer match the ground truth, does the code pass its tests. A verifier checks ground truth directly and isn't a proxy, so it is much harder to game than a learned reward model, and it works best in domains like math and code where correctness can be checked mechanically.

The optimiser is [GRPO](#c/grpo) (Group Relative Policy Optimization), from DeepSeek's earlier math work. For each problem the model samples a group of attempts, the verifier scores them, and each attempt is judged against the group's average. Better-than-average attempts are reinforced and worse ones suppressed. This removes the separate critic network that PPO needs, which cuts memory and compute a lot and is a major reason reasoning training spread so quickly across labs.

DeepSeek also reported an experimental variant, R1-Zero, trained by RL directly on the base model. The released R1 added a small amount of curated "cold-start" data and further stages to improve readability and general behaviour.

## The "aha moment"

The most discussed result was emergent behaviour. During RL training the model began, without being told to, to pause, re-examine its work and change approach mid-solution. DeepSeek called this an "aha moment". Nobody taught the model to write "wait, let me reconsider". The behaviour emerged from optimising for correct final answers over long reasoning chains. This is the mechanism behind the test-time-compute paradigm: RLVR teaches a model to make productive use of thinking at inference time.

## Distillation

DeepSeek then showed that R1's reasoning could be [distilled](#c/distillation) into much smaller open models, which were trained on R1's outputs. The direction matters. That is a lab distilling its *own* model downward, not copying a closed frontier model. The flagship case is closer to "RL produced reasoning, then distillation propagated it downward" than to "open models faked reasoning by copying GPT", which [challenges the idea](#c/c-distill-open) that distillation from closed models drives open reasoning gains.

## Reception and caveats

R1 made RLVR plus GRPO the default recipe for reasoning post-training and set off a wave of [GRPO variants](#c/grpo-variants) (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VAPO and others) aimed at length bias, exploration collapse and training stability. One of these, GSPO, specifically addresses stability problems when training MoE models.

Whether RLVR creates new reasoning ability is disputed. One careful study found that RLVR raises the probability of correct samples but narrows the set of problems a model can solve at all. On that reading it sharpens abilities the base model already had, and distillation is what transfers genuinely new patterns. R1's "aha moment" is the strongest evidence [on the other side](#c/c-rlvr-new). The truth probably depends on how "new" capability is defined.

## From the chat

- The chat described R1 as the landmark RLVR demonstration: "RLVR training can elicit sophisticated reasoning including an 'aha moment' where models spontaneously develop self-reflection."
- It explained GRPO's importance as mostly about cost, since dropping the critic network made reasoning training affordable.
- It corrected its own earlier claim that "a chunk" of open reasoning gains came from distillation. R1's headline result came largely *without* a frontier-distillation crutch, and DeepSeek distilled its own model downward.
- It flagged the RLVR-doesn't-create-new-ability study as "a serious, credible critique rather than settled fact."

deepseek-v32.overview: **DeepSeek-V3.2** (late 2025) keeps the [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) backbone: **671B total, 37B active**, 61 layers, 256 routed experts with 8 + 1 shared active, and [MLA](#c/mla). Its single architectural change, relative to V3.1-Terminus, is **[DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)](#c/dsa)**, added through continued training. A cheap "lightning indexer" scores earlier tokens, and full attention runs only over the selected top few, cutting attention cost from O(L²) to O(Lk). DeepSeek held the recipe fixed to isolate DSA, and the aim was parity, not a quality gain. It reports roughly 2–3× faster long-context processing, 30–40% less memory at 128K and a 50%+ API price cut, with nearly identical quality. The capability jump to GPT-5-comparable levels, with the V3.2-Speciale variant reporting IMO/IOI gold-medal performance, came from scaled RL post-training. Those comparisons are DeepSeek's own. V3.2 is the clearest example that [architecture wins are now mostly efficiency](#c/c-arch-efficiency).

llama4.overview: **Llama 4 Maverick** (Meta, April 2025) was Meta's first MoE generation: **400B total, 17B active**, 128 experts, 1M-token context, trained on about 22 trillion tokens. It takes a different MoE approach from DeepSeek. It uses **fewer, larger experts**, with 2 active per token at an 8,192 width against DeepSeek's 8 of 256 at 2,048, and it **alternates MoE and dense blocks** every other layer, where DeepSeek makes nearly every layer MoE. For attention it uses the standard [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa), not MLA. The chat called it the "conservative, classic MoE" reference point against DeepSeek's more aggressive design. It is natively multimodal and ships with a smaller sibling, [Llama 4 Scout](#c/llama4-scout). A later benchmark (Stanford HELM's IFEval) showed IBM's much smaller hybrid [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4) trailing only Maverick among open models.
llama4.article:
**Llama 4 Maverick** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model released by Meta in April 2025, alongside its smaller sibling [Llama 4 Scout](#c/llama4-scout). It was Meta's first MoE generation, after the dense Llama 1–3 line. Maverick has **400 billion total parameters with 17 billion active per token**, 128 experts and a 1-million-token context window, and was trained on about 22 trillion tokens. The chat described its design as the "conservative, classic MoE" counterpoint to [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3).

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Meta |
| Released | April 2025 |
| Total / active parameters | 400B / 17B |
| Experts | 128 |
| Active experts per token | 2, each 8,192 wide |
| MoE placement | Alternating MoE and dense layers |
| Attention | [Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)](#c/gqa) |
| Context | 1M tokens |
| Training data | ~22T tokens |

## A different MoE philosophy

Open MoE models in 2025 split on **expert granularity**. DeepSeek cut its FFN capacity into [many small experts](#c/fine-grained): 256 of them at a 2,048 intermediate width, with 8 routed plus 1 shared active per token. Llama 4 went the other way, with fewer and larger experts: 2 active per token at an 8,192 width. Meta's own description says each token goes to a shared expert plus one of the 128 routed experts. Either way, each Llama 4 expert is a much bigger slice of FFN.

The second difference is **where MoE appears**. DeepSeek-V3 makes every layer MoE except the first three. Llama 4 alternates MoE and dense blocks every other layer, so half its layers carry an ordinary dense FFN.

On attention, Llama 4 uses the industry-standard [GQA](#c/gqa), which shrinks the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) by sharing key/value heads across groups of query heads. It does not use DeepSeek's [MLA](#c/mla), which compresses more but is more complex.

## Why it matters

Maverick is a useful control case. It is a big, well-resourced MoE model that took the simpler path on every axis: coarser experts, a partly dense stack and default attention. Comparing it with DeepSeek-V3, [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) makes the design space clear. On the FFN side everyone converged on MoE but disagreed on granularity and shared experts. On the attention side the split is GQA (Llama 4, Qwen3) against MLA (DeepSeek, Kimi K2). The chat regarded its specs, like DeepSeek's, as the most trustworthy in the comparison because they come from real technical reports.

Maverick also serves as a benchmark reference. In Stanford HELM's IFEval instruction-following results, IBM's hybrid [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4)-H-Small beat every open-weight model except Maverick, a model more than twelve times its size (the chat quotes 402B for Maverick in that context).

## Trade-offs and limits

Few large experts give the router fewer combinations per token than fine-grained designs, and interleaving dense layers limits how far total capacity can grow for a given active budget. Maverick's sparsity ratio (17B of 400B, about 4%) is broadly similar to DeepSeek-V3's (37B of 671B, about 5.5%). Kimi K2 pushed further, to 32B of about 1T. As with every MoE model, all 400B parameters must be held in memory to serve it.

## Reception and caveats

The launch drew criticism when it emerged that the version at the top of the LMArena leaderboard was an experimental chat-tuned variant, not the released model. This fed a wider scepticism about vendor-reported benchmarks. The chat gives no benchmark figures for Maverick, and none are given here.

## From the chat

- The chat called Llama 4 "Meta's first MoE generation" and gave its specs: 400B total, 17B active, 128 experts, 1M context, ~22T tokens, April 2025.
- It set Llama 4 against DeepSeek as "a genuinely different MoE philosophy": fewer, larger experts (2 active at 8,192) against many small ones (2,048), and MoE every other layer against almost every layer.
- It described Llama 4's use of GQA as "the safe default".
- It noted that Llama 4's config would show `num_key_value_heads` well below `num_attention_heads`, unlike DeepSeek's MLA setup, where the two are equal.

llama4-scout.overview: **Llama 4 Scout** (Meta, April 2025) is the smaller sibling of [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4): a **109B-parameter** [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model whose standout feature is a **10-million-token context window**, ten times Maverick's 1M and far beyond most open models of its time. It uses the same family design, with [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa) for a smaller KV-cache and Meta's coarser MoE with fewer, larger experts. Per Meta it has 17B active parameters across 16 experts, and it was sized to run on a single high-end GPU host. At multi-million-token lengths the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) and attention cost dominate everything else, which is why techniques like GQA, [NoPE](#c/nope)-style positional changes and sparse or linear attention matter so much at that scale. How well Scout actually uses its full 10M context is less established than the headline number.

qwen3.overview: **Qwen3** (Alibaba, April 2025) is an open-weight model family widely regarded as the top open family in each size class. It includes dense models and MoE models, with the flagship **Qwen3-235B-A22B** (235B total, 22B active, 128 experts with 8 active per token) and a smaller 30B-A3B. For attention it uses the standard [GQA](#c/gqa). Its notable MoE decision is a subtraction: it [dropped the shared expert](#c/no-shared) that [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45) all kept, which makes it a live test of whether the always-on expert is needed. The family also introduced switchable thinking and non-thinking modes in one model. The weights are open, but the training data and full training pipeline are not.
qwen3.article:
**Qwen3** is a family of open-weight language models released by Alibaba's Qwen team in April 2025. It spans small dense models up to large [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) models, and it earned a reputation as the best open family in each size class. Its architectural significance is a deliberate **subtraction**: unlike the DeepSeek-style MoE designs of the time, Qwen3's MoE models have **no shared expert**.

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Alibaba (Qwen team) |
| Released | April 2025 |
| MoE flagship | Qwen3-235B-A22B (235B total, 22B active) |
| Smaller MoE | Qwen3-30B-A3B |
| Experts (flagship) | 128, 8 active per token |
| Shared expert | None |
| Attention | [Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)](#c/gqa) |
| Also | Dense models at smaller sizes |

The "A22B" naming states the active parameter count directly, which reflects how central the [total-versus-active split](#c/r-smaller) had become by 2025.

## Dropping the shared expert

DeepSeek's [fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained) design pairs many small routed experts with one always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) that handles processing nearly every token needs, so the routed experts don't each relearn it. By 2025 [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45) all kept a shared expert.

Qwen3 [removed it](#c/no-shared). Its MoE layers use only routed experts, still fine-grained, with 8 of 128 active in the flagship. Qwen3 ranked at the top of its size classes anyway, which is evidence that the shared expert is at least not essential. The chat described the question as "one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design right now." The field hasn't settled it.

## Attention

Qwen3 uses GQA, the standard choice that shrinks the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) by having groups of query heads share key/value heads. It does not use DeepSeek's [MLA](#c/mla), which compresses more but is more complex. In the 2025 landscape this puts Qwen3 with [Llama 4](#c/llama4) on attention, and with DeepSeek on fine-grained experts.

## Training and modes

Qwen3 models support a hybrid **thinking / non-thinking** mode. The same model can reason at length before answering or respond directly, so users can trade test-time compute for speed. This fits the wider 2025 shift in which capability gains came mainly from [post-training](#c/post-training) and reasoning RL, not from architecture changes. On post-training data, the chat cited the Qwen team's earlier (Qwen2) description of a hybrid pipeline: human annotation combined with automated data synthesis, with LLM judges used more and more for scale.

## Why it matters

Qwen3 is a clean natural experiment. It is a top-tier MoE family that removed a component its peers treated as standard, and it didn't pay an obvious price. With its strong results across sizes, that made it a default base for many open fine-tunes and derivative models.

## Trade-offs and caveats

Without a shared expert, the routed experts must cover common processing among themselves, which may make routing and balancing matter more. Whether dropping it helps, hurts or is neutral at a given scale hasn't been cleanly isolated in public. The chat also cautioned that its internal Qwen3 numbers leaned partly on third-party comparison write-ups. The headline counts are solid, but finer details such as exact layer and head counts should be checked against the model card.

## From the chat

- The chat called Qwen3 "widely regarded as the top-tier open-weight family by size class."
- Its highlighted MoE decision was dropping the shared expert, described as "a live experiment in whether the always-on shared expert is actually necessary."
- It placed Qwen3 on the GQA side of the attention split, with Llama 4, against MLA in DeepSeek and Kimi K2.
- It cautioned that the finer Qwen3 specs came partly from secondhand roundups and deliberately gave no layer or head counts.

kimi-k2.overview: **Kimi K2** (Moonshot AI, July 2025) is the sparsity standout of the open MoE landscape: **about 1 trillion total parameters with only 32B active** per token (roughly 3%), spread over **384 experts**. That pushes the "huge total, small active" ratio further than almost any other open model. It borrows from the DeepSeek lineage, using [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla) instead of GQA and keeping DeepSeek's [fine-grained + shared expert](#c/fine-grained) layout, with 8 routed experts plus a shared one per token. Moonshot trained it with its MuonClip optimizer and positioned it for agentic and tool-use work. The chat flagged that its specs came partly from comparison roundups, not a first-party report it could verify, so the exact figures are well attested but secondhand. Its sibling [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear) tests linear attention at smaller scale.
kimi-k2.article:
**Kimi K2** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model released by the Chinese lab Moonshot AI in July 2025. At about **one trillion total parameters with only 32 billion active per token**, it is the sparsest of the major open flagships. It stores roughly 30 times more parameters than it uses on any given token. Architecturally it follows [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) closely, and the chat called it "the scale standout" of the 2025 open landscape.

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Moonshot AI |
| Released | July 2025 |
| Total / active parameters | ~1T / 32B |
| Routed experts | 384 |
| Active experts per token | 8 routed + 1 shared |
| Shared expert | Yes |
| Attention | [Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)](#c/mla) |

Compared with DeepSeek-V3 (256 experts, 671B total, 37B active), K2 adds more experts and more total capacity while cutting active parameters slightly. That is the MoE bet in its purest form: grow knowledge capacity, keep per-token cost flat.

## Design lineage

K2 shows how quickly open-model techniques spread. It takes two defining DeepSeek choices:

- **[MLA](#c/mla)** compresses keys and values into a small cached latent, giving a much smaller [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) than the standard [GQA](#c/gqa) used by Llama 4 and Qwen3.
- **[Fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained)**: many small routed experts plus an always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) dropped the shared expert, but K2 kept it.

Moonshot's main training change was the optimizer. It trained K2 with **MuonClip**, a variant of the Muon optimizer with a mechanism to keep attention logits from blowing up. Moonshot presented this as the key to stable pre-training at trillion-parameter scale.

## Why it matters

K2 is the extreme data point on the sparsity axis. It shows that a model can be pushed to a trillion parameters while its per-token arithmetic stays comparable to models a third its size, which is exactly why [frontier size and serving cost came apart](#c/r-smaller). It was also positioned for agentic use (tool calling and multi-step tasks), the area where post-training was moving fastest in 2025–26.

## Trade-offs and limits

Extreme sparsity keeps compute cheap but not memory. All ~1T parameters must be held in accelerator memory to serve the model, which makes it expensive to host even though each token is cheap to compute. With 384 experts, all-to-all communication and load balancing are also harder when experts are spread across many GPUs.

## The Kimi Linear direction

Moonshot also released [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), a much smaller 48B model that uses full attention (MLA) in only one of every four layers and a cheaper linear "Delta Attention" in the rest, with no positional encoding in its full-attention layers. The chat pointed to whether Moonshot adopts that approach for its next flagship (K3) as a decisive test of whether [linear attention](#c/linear-attn) works at production scale.

## From the chat

- The chat called K2 "the scale standout": 1T total, 32B active, 384 experts, pushing the sparsity ratio "further than almost anyone."
- It noted that K2 borrows MLA "from the DeepSeek lineage rather than using GQA" and keeps the shared expert.
- It warned that K2's specs came partly from comparison roundups, not a first-party report it could verify: "well-attested-but-secondhand."
- It raised the future K3 flagship as the test of whether Kimi Linear's hybrid attention reaches flagship scale.

kimi-linear.overview: **Kimi Linear** (Moonshot AI, 2025) is a **48B-parameter** MoE model with about 3B active. It is Moonshot's test of [linear / hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn). Only **one in four layers** uses full attention, and those use [MLA](#c/mla). The other three use a linear "Delta Attention" (Kimi Delta Attention) whose cost grows linearly with sequence length and whose state doesn't grow the way a [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) does. Its full-attention blocks drop explicit positional encoding entirely ([NoPE](#c/nope)) and leave position to the linear layers, which helps when extending to very long contexts. It reports competitive quality at much higher throughput. It is still a mid-sized model, though, and whether the approach holds at flagship scale, for instance in Moonshot's next flagship after [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2), was flagged as one of the decisive open questions for linear attention.

glm-45.overview: **GLM-4.5** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, July 2025) is a **355B-total, 32B-active** [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model and the direct predecessor of the [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) line. In MoE design it sided with DeepSeek: like [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) and [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) it **kept a shared expert**, while [Qwen3 dropped it](#c/no-shared), which is why the chat cites it in the shared-expert debate. It was released as open weights and aimed at reasoning, coding and agentic use, the direction the whole GLM family has followed since. The family then moved fast: GLM-4.6 in September 2025, then 4.7, then GLM-5 in February 2026, which roughly doubled the size to 744B total and 40B active. The chat gives few further architectural details for GLM-4.5 itself.

glm-5.overview: **GLM-5** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, February 2026) is an open-weight, MIT-licensed MoE flagship: **744B total, ~40B active**, with 256 experts and 8 active per token (about 5.9% sparsity), trained on 28.5T tokens and scaled up from GLM-4.5's 355B/32B. It takes [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa) wholesale from [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32), and its architecture is literally named `glm_moe_dsa`. It reduces depth to **80 layers** to cut expert-parallel communication. Its main novelty is post-training, an asynchronous RL system called **slime** that decouples generation from training for large-scale agentic RL. Reports say it was trained on about 100,000 Huawei Ascend chips with no Nvidia hardware, which was initially unconfirmed. It [self-reports](#c/vendor-claims) 77.8% on SWE-bench Verified, about 3 points behind Claude Opus 4.6. Context is 200K in, about 128K out.
glm-5.article:
**GLM-5** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) language model released by Zhipu AI (Z.ai) in February 2026. It is the flagship of a fast-moving family (GLM-4.5, 4.6, 4.7, then 5, 5-Turbo, [5.1](#c/glm-51) and [5.2](#c/glm-52)), and it is the one with a real technical report. Its construction shows two trends of the period clearly: architecture techniques spreading quickly between labs, and the most novel engineering moving from the transformer to the post-training pipeline.

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Zhipu AI (Z.ai) |
| Released | February 2026 |
| Total / active parameters | 744B / ~40B |
| Experts | 256, 8 active per token (~5.9% sparsity) |
| Layers | 80 |
| Attention | [DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)](#c/dsa) |
| Pre-training data | 28.5T tokens |
| Context | 200K input, up to ~128K output |
| License | MIT, open weights |

It grew from [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45)'s 355B total and 32B active, roughly doubling total parameters while adding only about 8B active.

## Importing DeepSeek Sparse Attention

GLM-5 did not build its own long-context mechanism. It adopted [DSA](#c/dsa), introduced months earlier in [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32), and its architecture identifier, `glm_moe_dsa`, says so openly. DSA uses a cheap "lightning indexer" to score earlier tokens and runs attention only over the most relevant ones, bringing attention cost down from quadratic toward linear in sequence length. The report presents DSA as what made scaling to 744B parameters and 28.5T tokens affordable. Coverage compared the adoption to how models took up [RoPE](#c/rope) once it was published.

## Depth traded for communication

GLM-5 uses 256 experts but cuts its layer count to 80 in order to **reduce expert-parallelism communication**. In a large MoE, experts sit on different GPUs and every MoE layer sends tokens across the network to reach them. Fewer layers mean fewer of these exchanges. It is a concrete case of the depth–width–expert-count trade-off being settled partly by serving and systems constraints, not by model quality alone.

## Post-training: slime

As the chat put it, "the post-training story is the headline, not the architecture." GLM-5's main engineering contribution is **slime**, an asynchronous RL infrastructure. Standard RL for LLMs runs generate, score and update steps one after another, so at 744B scale GPUs sit idle in one phase while another runs. Slime separates generation from training so both run continuously. It is aimed at **agentic** training: runs reportedly produce 3,000–6,000 messages (about 60–100M output tokens) to train long-range planning and tool use. It builds on the [RLVR](#c/rlvr) wave, extended to long-horizon agent trajectories where rewards are harder to define.

## Hardware

Several sources report that GLM-5 was trained on about **100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B** chips using the MindSpore framework, with no Nvidia hardware. That is significant given Zhipu's placement on the US Entity List. One careful source noted the training hardware was not officially confirmed at first, so the claim is plausible and widely repeated but should be treated with some caution.

## Benchmarks and caveats

Zhipu reported **77.8% on SWE-bench Verified**, 62% on BrowseComp, first place on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and reduced hallucination. More balanced coverage put it about 3 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 on SWE-bench Verified and about 9 points behind on Terminal-Bench 2.0: competitive with the closed frontier on agentic coding, and leading among open models, but not on top. These are mostly self-reported [vendor claims](#c/vendor-claims), and independent verification was still pending.

## From the chat

- The chat anchored on GLM-5 over newer versions because it has "a real technical report (the arXiv source)". Details for 5.1 and later came only from thin secondary sources.
- It called the DSA adoption "the clearest illustration of the 'techniques diffuse fast' point": one lab's late-2025 innovation became a second flagship's backbone within months.
- It highlighted the 80-layer choice as a "real systems-level architecture decision" driven by expert-parallel communication cost.
- It trusted the report's construction facts (744B/40B, 256 experts top-8, DSA, 80 layers, slime, 28.5T tokens) but wanted independent confirmation of the hardware claims and benchmark comparisons.

glm-51.overview: **GLM-5.1** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, late March 2026) is an incremental update on the [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) base. By the available accounts it keeps the same shape: a **744B-total, ~40B-active** [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) with 256 experts, 8 active per token, and [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa). Its headline claim is that it scores **94.6% of Claude Opus 4.6's coding score**. That figure is self-reported and not independently verified, and the chat found it only in a single SEO-oriented blog that itself flagged the numbers as unverified [vendor claims](#c/vendor-claims). It arrived alongside GLM-5-Turbo during a period when the GLM family was releasing new versions every few weeks. It was later followed by [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52), which added a 1M-token context. Beyond these points the chat had little verified detail on what changed from GLM-5 to 5.1.

glm-52.overview: **GLM-5.2** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, released June 13, 2026) adds a **1-million-token context** over [GLM-5.1](#c/glm-51), about 5× the GLM-5 line's 200K, with up to 131,072 output tokens. It also adds two reasoning-effort presets, **High** and **Max**, with Max recommended for coding. It launched on every GLM Coding Plan tier, with MIT-licensed open weights to follow. Coverage contradicts itself. [Early reports (June 13–15)](#c/glm52-early) said no benchmarks were published at all. [Later reports (June 16–17)](#c/glm52-late) claimed it [beats GPT-5.5 on long-horizon coding](#c/c-glm52) at one-sixth the cost, and even that it beat Claude Fable 5 in blind tests. Treat these as unverified vendor claims. Parameter count is reported as 753B, against 744B for 5.1, which could be a real change or loose reporting. With no technical report, how the 1M context was achieved is unknown.

smollm3.overview: **SmolLM3** (Hugging Face, 2025) is a small, fully open **3B-parameter dense** model. It appears in this landscape for its attention design, not its size. It uses [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa) with **periodic [NoPE](#c/nope) layers**: roughly every fourth layer drops rotary positional encoding and relies on the causal mask alone to convey token order, while the other layers keep [RoPE](#c/rope). The aim is better behaviour when extending to long contexts, since layers without explicit positions don't hit unfamiliar position values past the training length. Hugging Face also published its training recipe in unusual detail. The chat mentions it only briefly, as a small-model example of NoPE alongside [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), and notes that removing positional encoding had not yet become standard in any major flagship.
